formation.title: The United Pueblo Rises
formation.text:
For generations, the peoples of the desert Southwest have lived in their multistory adobe settlements, Keres at Acoma and Laguna, Tanoan speakers along the Rio Grande, Zuni in their ancient stronghold, Hopi on the distant mesas. Each pueblo governed itself through councils of elders and clan mothers, united by the kachina traditions that bind earth to sky. Now, for the first time, the pueblos have chosen to stand together as one nation. The question before the council is not whether to unite, but what the United Pueblo shall become. Some invoke the memory of Popé, whose knotted cord once rallied every pueblo against a common enemy. Others speak of the kiva: the underground heart where knowledge is preserved and the ceremonies that sustain the world are performed. Both paths lead to strength, but of different kinds.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: We shall be as Popé, unyielding in defense of our people.

modifiers.name: Path of Popé
modifiers.text: In the spirit of Popé, the Tewa leader who united the pueblos against Spanish tyranny, the United Pueblo embraces the warrior tradition. No foreign power shall subjugate these lands again.

options.text: The kiva endures. Our strength flows from sacred tradition.

modifiers.name: Path of the Kiva
modifiers.text: The kiva endures beneath the earth as it always has. Through ceremony, sacred knowledge, and the bonds of clan and moiety, the United Pueblo will preserve its ancient ways and flourish in wisdom.

advances.name: Pueblo Defensive Architecture
advances.text: The ancestral Pueblo builders constructed multi-story adobe complexes with no ground-level doors or windows. Entry was via ladders through roof hatches, which could be pulled up during attacks.

advances.name: Desert Archery
advances.text: Pueblo bow warriors developed techniques suited to the arid landscape, using the terrain of mesas, canyons, and arroyos to maximum defensive advantage.

advances.name: Acequia Irrigation
advances.text: Communal gravity-fed irrigation canals diverted water from the Rio Grande and its tributaries to fields of maize, beans, squash, cotton, and tobacco.

advances.name: Kiva Tradition
advances.text: The kiva, a subterranean ceremonial chamber, served as the religious, political, and social heart of each pueblo, where sacred knowledge was preserved and transmitted.

advances.name: Turquoise Trade
advances.text: Pueblo artisans inherited the turquoise-working traditions of Chaco Canyon, producing ornaments, pendants, and inlaid objects for trade across the Southwest and beyond.

event.title: The Turquoise Road
event.text:
Long before the pueblos bore their current names, the ancient peoples of Chaco Canyon built a trade network spanning hundreds of miles. Over fifty thousand pieces of turquoise have been found in the walls of Pueblo Bonito alone, more than at every other archaeological site in the Southwest combined. The blue-green stone traveled along roads remarkably straight and wide, connecting outlying communities to the ceremonial center. Macaw feathers came north from Mesoamerica; shells arrived from the Pacific coast; copper bells from distant workshops.

Though Chaco itself fell silent centuries ago, the knowledge of these roads and the art of turquoise working never vanished. The pueblo artisans of Keres, Zuni, and Hopi maintain the tradition, cutting and polishing stone with techniques passed down through generations. The revival of these trade connections offers a choice.

options.text: Turquoise is wealth. Let the trade flow and enrich our people.

modifiers.name: Turquoise Road, Commerce
modifiers.text: The revival of the ancient turquoise trade routes brings wealth flowing through pueblo workshops and marketplaces.

options.text: Turquoise is legacy. Let its beauty speak our name to the world.

modifiers.name: Turquoise Road, Prestige
modifiers.text: The distinctive blue-green stone of the pueblos has become a mark of status and sophistication across the trade networks, elevating the Pueblo name.

advances.name: Clan Governance
advances.text: Pueblo communities were governed through interlocking clan and moiety systems. Decisions were made by councils of elders representing each clan, ensuring stability through consensus.

advances.name: Multi-Story Pueblos
advances.text: Pueblo architects refined techniques for constructing four- and five-story adobe and sandstone apartment complexes, housing hundreds of families in integrated communities.

advances.name: Pueblo Pottery Mastery
advances.text: The distinctive black-on-white and polychrome pottery traditions of the pueblos reached new heights of artistry, with each village developing recognizable styles.

advances.name: Communal Militia
advances.text: Pueblo defense was organized through the moiety system, with each half of the community responsible for raising and training warriors to protect the settlement.

advances.name: Waffle Gardens
advances.text: The Zuni perfected the waffle garden, sunken grid beds surrounded by low earthen walls that captured and conserved precious moisture in the arid landscape.

advances.name: Kachina Ceremonies
advances.text: The elaborate cycle of masked kachina dances represented hundreds of spirit beings, each tied to specific aspects of rainfall, fertility, healing, and the cosmic order.

event.title: The Dance of the Kachinas
event.text:
Deep in the subterranean kiva, the masked dancers have emerged. The kachina ceremony (the cycle of dances that brings rain to the fields, health to the people, and harmony between the living and the spirits) has reached its full expression across the United Pueblo. In the western pueblos, Hopi and Zuni dancers wear elaborately carved and painted masks representing hundreds of different kachina spirits, each with a specific role in the cosmic order. In the eastern pueblos along the Rio Grande, the ceremonies take on their own character, blending with the moiety system that divides each community into complementary halves.

The kachina tradition is more than religion. It is the mechanism by which newcomers are integrated into pueblo life, disputes are settled through ritual rather than violence, and the agricultural calendar is maintained. The emergence of the dancers from the kiva is the emergence of order from chaos, of community from scattered families.

options.text: The kachinas dance. The world is renewed.

advances.name: Pueblo Trade Fairs
advances.text: Seasonal gatherings at major pueblos served as trade fairs where pottery, turquoise, cotton textiles, foodstuffs, and goods from distant regions changed hands.

advances.name: Warrior Societies
advances.text: Each pueblo maintained warrior societies tied to the kachina tradition. Initiates underwent rigorous training and ceremonial preparation before serving as guardians of the community.

advances.name: Mesa Scout Tradition
advances.text: Swift runners and scouts trained to navigate the vast desert terrain between pueblos, serving as both messengers and reconnaissance forces against approaching threats.

advances.name: Oral Traditions
advances.text: Sacred narratives, astronomical knowledge, agricultural calendars, and historical memory were preserved through elaborate oral traditions passed from elders to initiates within the kivas.

advances.name: Cotton Weaving
advances.text: Pueblo weavers cultivated cotton in irrigated fields and produced textiles of remarkable quality, using natural dyes and complex patterns for both domestic use and trade.

advances.name: Inter-Pueblo Council
advances.text: As the pueblos drew closer together, representatives from each community began meeting in formal council to coordinate defense, manage shared water resources, and settle disputes.

advances.name: Mesa Fortification
advances.text: The Hopi and other western pueblos built their settlements atop sheer mesas, creating natural fortresses accessible only by steep, narrow paths easily defended against any attacker.

advances.name: The Pueblo Revolt
advances.text: In 1680, Popé of Ohkay Owingeh organized the most successful indigenous uprising in American history, coordinating attacks across dozens of pueblos to drive out Spanish colonial rule.

event.title: The Knotted Cord
event.text:
In the summer of 1680, the leader Popé sent runners to every pueblo carrying knotted cords. Each knot marked a day remaining until the coordinated uprising against Spanish colonial rule. When the cords ran out, the pueblos rose as one. Popé, a Tewa medicine man from Ohkay Owingeh who had been flogged and imprisoned for practicing the old religion, had built a secret alliance spanning hundreds of miles, from Taos in the north to the Hopi mesas far to the west. The revolt killed four hundred Spaniards and drove the remaining two thousand settlers south to El Paso. For twelve years, the pueblos governed themselves, tearing down churches, restoring kivas, and reviving the kachina ceremonies that the Spanish had tried to destroy. It was the most successful indigenous uprising against European colonialism in the Americas.

The spirit of that day lives on. How shall we honor the legacy of Popé and the warriors who fought beside him?

options.text: The knotted cord binds us still: our unity is our weapon.

modifiers.name: Spirit of the Revolt, Unity
modifiers.text: The coordinated uprising has forged the pueblos into a single fighting force, ready to defend their homeland against any aggressor.

options.text: We fought to restore our sacred ways. Let them flourish again.

modifiers.name: Spirit of the Revolt, Restoration
modifiers.text: With foreign altars torn down and the kachina masks brought back into the light, the ancient ways have been restored to their rightful place.

advances.name: Spiritual Restoration
advances.text: After the revolt, Popé traveled from pueblo to pueblo ordering the destruction of churches, the restoration of kivas, and the revival of banned kachina ceremonies.

advances.name: Guerrilla Tactics
advances.text: The revolt demonstrated Pueblo mastery of guerrilla warfare, simultaneous attacks, scorched earth, and exploitation of the desert terrain that no foreign army could navigate.

advances.name: Horse Adoption
advances.text: The Spanish retreat left behind horses that transformed Pueblo mobility. Herds are kept and bred beside the pueblos, and Pueblo warriors quickly master mounted warfare, combining it with their existing knowledge of desert combat.

advances.name: Pueblo Confederacy
advances.text: The multi-pueblo alliance forged by Popé's revolt (spanning Tewa, Tiwa, Towa, Keres, Zuni, and Hopi) proved that the autonomous pueblos could act as a unified nation when survival demanded it.

advances.name: Trade Restoration
advances.text: With colonial restrictions lifted, traditional trade networks between pueblos and with neighboring peoples were rebuilt, restoring the flow of turquoise, pottery, textiles, and foodstuffs.

advances.name: Unified Council
advances.text: A permanent council of representatives from all pueblos formalized the ad hoc alliances of the revolt era into a standing institution for collective governance.

advances.name: Enduring Resistance
advances.text: The memory of the revolt and the twelve years of self-rule that followed instilled a tradition of disciplined, unyielding resistance to any external threat.

advances.name: Advanced Irrigation
advances.text: Expanded acequia networks, improved check dams, and refined water management techniques allowed the pueblos to support larger populations in the arid Southwest.

advances.name: Pueblo Artistic Renaissance
advances.text: New pottery styles, finer inlay of shell and turquoise, and the weaving of wool from Spanish sheep marked a flowering of Pueblo artistic expression.

advances.name: Mounted Warrior Tradition
advances.text: The adoption of horses from the Spanish retreat gave rise to a new tradition of mounted desert warfare, combining Pueblo knowledge of the terrain with cavalry mobility.

advances.name: Diplomatic Pragmatism
advances.text: Pueblo leaders learned to play colonial powers against each other, extract favorable terms through negotiation, and maintain autonomy through shrewd diplomacy rather than force alone.

advances.name: Pueblo Sovereignty
advances.text: The assertion of Pueblo nationhood (the right to self-governance, territorial integrity, and cultural self-determination) as a matter of established principle rather than aspiration.

advances.name: Cultural Preservation
advances.text: In the face of modernization and external pressures, the pueblos committed to the deliberate preservation of language, ceremony, craft traditions, and communal land tenure.

advances.name: Peace with the Comanche
advances.text: By the peace of 1786 the Comanche cease to raid the pueblos and come to trade instead. Hides, horses and trade metal are exchanged for maize, blankets and turquoise, and from 1821 wagons from Missouri come down the trail to Santa Fe.

advances.name: Land and Water Rights
advances.text: Securing formal recognition of communal land tenure and ancestral water rights along the Rio Grande and its tributaries, ensuring the material foundation of Pueblo life.

advances.name: Confederal Constitution
advances.text: A written framework codifying the relationship between autonomous pueblos, establishing shared institutions while preserving each community's right to self-governance.

advances.name: Standing Army
advances.text: The evolution of Pueblo warrior societies into a professional defense force, combining traditional knowledge of desert warfare with modern military organization. Each pueblo keeps a company under its war captain, ready to join the others on campaign.

destiny.name: Destiny of the United Pueblo
destiny.text: The pueblos stand united. With stability secured, the council must decide the path forward: whether through the strength of Pope's legacy or the wisdom of the kiva.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: The Destiny of the United Pueblo
event.text: The council fires burn bright in every pueblo from the Rio Grande to the distant mesas. For the first time in living memory, the autonomous communities have chosen to act as one nation. The elders have debated, the clan mothers have spoken, and the decision is made. The United Pueblo will endure, but its destiny remains to be written. The path chosen at formation now unfolds before us.

destiny.name: The Warpath
destiny.text: Secure the lands of the Dine and the Nde. No people who threaten the pueblos shall remain unchallenged on the borders of our homeland. Bring Dinetah and the Apache heartland under Pueblo control.

conditions.text: Chose Path of Popé
Own Dinétah, or a subject owns it
Own Natahéndé, or a subject owns it

event.title: Warpath of the Pueblos
event.text: The warriors of the United Pueblo have secured the borderlands. Dinetah, homeland of the Dine, and the Apache territory to the south now fall under the protection of the confederation. The knotted cord of Pope binds not just pueblo to pueblo, but extends outward to encompass all who would live in peace under the council's authority. Those who raid our fields and threaten our people have been brought to heel.

destiny.name: Council of War Chiefs
destiny.text: The great canyon of the Colorado and the eastern plains must fall under Pueblo authority. The war chiefs call the men of every pueblo into the communal militia, and the neighbors learn respect.

conditions.text: Own Havasubaaja, or a subject owns it
Own Tucumcari, or a subject owns it
Renaissance or later
Prestige at least 50

event.title: Desert War Council
event.text: The war chiefs of every pueblo have gathered in council. The confederation's warriors have pushed beyond the heartland, seizing the great canyon and the eastern plains. The militia of every pueblo answers the call. Now the council must decide how to press the advantage. Some advocate raids deep into enemy territory, enriching the pueblos with captured goods. Others urge the construction of a defensive network (watchtowers and mesa fortresses) to hold what has been won.

options.text: We raid. The spoils will strengthen our people.

modifiers.name: Raiders of the Mesa
modifiers.text: Pueblo war parties strike deep into enemy territory, returning with spoils that enrich the confederation, though the influx of foreign goods drives prices upward.

options.text: We fortify. The desert itself will be our shield.

modifiers.name: Desert Shield
modifiers.text: A network of mesa fortresses and watchtowers makes the Pueblo heartland virtually impregnable, though maintaining these defenses strains the treasury.

destiny.name: The Turquoise Eagle
destiny.text: The eagle soars over the entire Southwest. Bring the Mojave crossing, the Akimel heartland, and the southern hunting grounds into the confederation. Only renown as great as the land can hold such an empire.

conditions.text: Own Kwatsaan, or a subject owns it
Own Akimeḍ, or a subject owns it
Own Mah'hom, or a subject owns it
Prestige at least 75

event.title: The Turquoise Eagle
event.text: The confederation now stretches from the Mojave crossing in the west to the plains in the east, from the great canyon in the north to the Akimel lands in the south. Signal fires pass from mesa to mesa across it. The turquoise eagle (symbol of Pueblo power and the desert sky) flies over an empire. The council must decide the character of this new power. Shall the United Pueblo be a war eagle, striking fear into all who oppose it? Or shall its strength be the unbreakable endurance that has sustained the pueblos for centuries?

options.text: We are the war eagle. None shall stand against us.

modifiers.name: War Eagle
modifiers.text: The turquoise eagle strikes terror into the enemies of the pueblos. Foreign powers recognize the confederation's military might and grant favorable terms at the negotiating table.

options.text: We endure. That is our greatest strength.

modifiers.name: Indomitable Spirit
modifiers.text: The spirit of endurance that sustained the pueblos through centuries of hardship now manifests as an unyielding defensive tradition. Allies rally to the banner of the indomitable pueblo.

destiny.name: The Sacred Way
destiny.text: The kachina dancers of Orayvi have preserved the oldest ceremonies. Bring the Hopi mesas into the confederation and build the wealth needed to sustain the sacred traditions.

event.title: The Sacred Way Opens
event.text: The Hopi mesas (Orayvi, Walpi, Shungopavi) have joined the confederation, bringing with them the most ancient and elaborate kachina traditions in the Southwest. The treasury is growing as turquoise and pottery flow through the trade networks. The Sacred Way stretches forward: a path of wisdom, ceremony, and patient accumulation of wealth and knowledge.

destiny.name: The Artisan Age
destiny.text: Pueblo pottery is prized across the trade networks. Ensure pottery flows through our markets, fill the treasury, and open turquoise workshops in three pueblos to carry the artisan renaissance.

Pottery is traded in the market

event.title: The Pueblo Artisan Renaissance
event.text: The workshops of the United Pueblo are flourishing. Pottery painted with ancient symbols, turquoise set in shell, cotton woven in intricate patterns: Pueblo artisanship has become a source of wealth and pride. Turquoise workshops stand in the rooms of every great pueblo. The council must decide how to direct this renaissance. Some advocate expanding trade networks to bring Pueblo goods to distant markets. Others wish to attract foreign scholars and artisans, absorbing new techniques while preserving the core traditions.

options.text: Our crafts will be known in every market.

modifiers.name: Ceramic Masters
modifiers.text: Pueblo pottery commands premium prices in markets across the continent, drawing traders and expanding the confederation's diplomatic reach, though success breeds ease and the men of the workshops are slow to answer a muster.

options.text: We will learn from all peoples.

modifiers.name: Desert Scholars
modifiers.text: Foreign artisans and scholars are welcomed into the pueblos, bringing new techniques and ideas that blend with ancient traditions to produce remarkable innovations.

destiny.name: The Eternal Kiva
destiny.text: Build the Great Kiva, a ceremonial center worthy of a nation. Secure Halona Idiwana, fill the coffers, earn the world's respect, and keep kivas in five pueblos, where sacred knowledge is passed from the elders to the young for all time.

conditions.text: Own Halona Idiwan'a, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 3000
Prestige at least 75
At least 5 of our locations have a Kiva

event.title: The Eternal Kiva
event.text: The Great Kiva stands complete, a monumental ceremonial center unlike anything built since the days of Chaco Canyon. Below the earth, in the sacred chamber, the kachina dancers perform the ceremonies that renew the world. Above, the elders of every pueblo meet to keep the oral traditions, knowledge that has been passed from mouth to ear for a thousand years. The council gathers to consecrate this achievement. Shall the Eternal Kiva be a beacon of spiritual harmony, welcoming all peoples? Or shall it stand as proof that the Pueblo way of governance and community has produced something truly great?

options.text: The kiva welcomes all who seek harmony.

modifiers.name: Eternal Ceremonies
modifiers.text: The kachina ceremonies of the Great Kiva draw pilgrims from every nation. The spiritual harmony of the pueblos becomes a model for peaceful coexistence among diverse peoples.

options.text: The Pueblo way has proven its mastery.

modifiers.name: Pueblo Mastery
modifiers.text: The Great Kiva stands as proof that the Pueblo way (communal governance, sacred tradition, patient craft) has produced a civilization worthy of the world's respect.

units.name: Pueblo Bow Warriors
units.text: Skilled desert archers who exploit the mesas, canyons, and arroyos of the Southwest, these warriors defend pueblo settlements with deadly accuracy.

units.name: Pueblo Levy Warriors
units.text: Communal militia raised from the pueblo settlements through the moiety system. Stubborn defenders who fight hardest when protecting their homes.

units.name: Kachina Guardians
units.text: Elite warriors drawn from the ceremonial warrior societies, sanctified by kachina ritual. Their presence on the battlefield inspires extraordinary courage.

units.name: Mesa Scouts
units.text: Swift desert runners who navigate the vast distances between pueblos, serving as scouts and messengers. They know every canyon, arroyo, and hidden water source.

units.name: Revolt Warriors
units.text: Guerrilla fighters inspired by the spirit of Popé's 1680 uprising, specializing in coordinated ambushes and exploitation of desert terrain.

units.name: Pueblo Mounted Warriors
units.text: Pueblo cavalry trained in the desert warfare tradition, combining ancestral knowledge of the terrain with the mobility of horses acquired after the Spanish retreat.

units.name: War Captain's Company
units.text: The contingent a pueblo sends to a joint campaign under its own war captain. A few dozen men who march a dry country on little and do not break, as the pueblo companies did on every expedition against the raiders of the plains.

buildings.name: Kiva
buildings.text: A subterranean ceremonial chamber where the sacred dances are performed, political decisions are made, and the oral traditions that bind the community are transmitted to each new generation.

buildings.name: Turquoise Workshop
buildings.text: An artisan center where turquoise, shell, and copper are worked into pendants, beads, and inlaid ornaments using techniques inherited from the master craftspeople of Chaco Canyon.

buildings.name: Pueblo Granary
buildings.text: Communal food storage rooms within the multi-story adobe complex, sealed against vermin and moisture. The shared granary ensures that no family goes hungry when the harvest is poor.

buildings.name: Pueblo Fortress
buildings.text: A multi-story adobe defensive complex with no ground-level entrances. Access is by ladder through roof hatches that can be pulled up in moments, turning the entire structure into a fortress.

buildings.name: Pottery Workshop
buildings.text: A center for the production of Pueblo black-on-white and polychrome ceramics, where artisans shape, paint, and fire pottery using techniques refined over centuries.

buildings.name: Cotton Weaving Hall
buildings.text: A center for Pueblo textile production where cotton cultivated in irrigated fields is spun and woven on the upright loom into mantas, kilts and sashes, then painted, embroidered or striped with natural dyes in complex geometric patterns. Plain cloth is woven in every household; what the hall makes is the decorated cloth the pueblos traded.

buildings.name: Mesa Watchtower
buildings.text: A stone observation tower perched atop a mesa, part of a network of signal stations that allows the pueblos to coordinate their defense across vast distances.

buildings.name: Trade Fair Ground
buildings.text: A seasonal gathering place where pueblos and neighboring peoples exchange pottery, turquoise, cotton textiles, foodstuffs, and goods from across the trade networks.

buildings.name: Waffle Garden
buildings.text: The Zuni kitchen garden: sunken squares walled with clay that hold what little rain falls, each one watered by hand from a jar. It feeds a pueblo where a field would fail.

buildings.name: Horse Herd
buildings.text: A herd bred from the horses left behind in 1680 and pastured beside the pueblo. What the pueblo does not ride is traded on to the peoples of the plains.

children.text: Horses is produced in the market
Horses is traded in the market

buildings.name: War Council Hall
buildings.text: A fortified council hall where the war chiefs of every pueblo gather to coordinate the confederation's military campaigns, plan defenses, and mobilize warriors across the Southwest.

buildings.name: Great Kiva
buildings.text: A monumental subterranean ceremonial chamber rivaling the great kivas of ancient Chaco Canyon, where the most sacred dances are performed and the oral traditions of every pueblo are preserved.

list.name: Cacique and War Captain
list.text: The structural division of Pueblo authority into an inside ritual-political chief (the cacique, in Tewa the po'kwingeh) and an outside military chief (the war captain, in Tewa the t'owa e'). The cacique held office for life, was confirmed by the religious societies, and concerned himself with the ceremonial calendar, the planting and harvest, and the inner peace of the pueblo. The war captain was selected annually (often by the cacique with the moieties' counsel), held the right of warriors and the policing of the village, and took the field in the season of raid against Apache, Navajo, and Spanish encroachers. The two offices checked each other: the war captain could not undertake war without the cacique's concurrence and the ritual sanction of the societies, and the cacique could not police the village without the war captain's hand.

list.name: Kiva Council Chamber
list.text: The subterranean ceremonial room that served as the political-religious heart of every pueblo. Entered by ladder through the roof opening that represented the sipapu of emergence, the kiva housed the religious societies (the kachina cult, the medicine societies, the warrior fraternities) and was where the cacique convened the village's elders for matters of consequence: the calendar of feasts, the assignment of irrigation water, the judgement of grave wrongs, the ratification of war. Each pueblo had several kivas, divided by moiety or by society membership; the great kivas of Chaco-era construction (Pueblo Bonito, Aztec, Casa Rinconada) held more than a hundred. The kiva was simultaneously sacred precinct, council chamber, weaving workshop, and men's lodge.

list.name: Moiety Dual System
list.text: The social-political division of each pueblo into two complementary halves that alternated authority by season. Among the Tewa pueblos these were the Summer People and the Winter People, each with its own cacique, its own kiva, and its own calendar of feasts. Among the Hopi the analogous division ran Squash / Turquoise. Authority for the public business of the pueblo (assigning fields, calling work parties, mounting hunts) passed from one moiety to the other at the equinoxes, so that no single faction held the village year-round. The moieties were exogamous: a Summer man married a Winter woman, and the children took the mother's moiety, weaving the village together by kinship while keeping its public faces alternating.

list.name: Knotted Cord Runner Network
list.text: The cross-pueblo coordination institution descended from Po'pay's organization of the 1680 Pueblo Revolt. From his refuge at Taos the Tewa religious leader sent runners south and west bearing knotted yucca-fibre cords with a knot for each day remaining until the rising; pueblos accepted the cord by untying knots in turn. On the agreed day, August 10, 1680, Tewa, Tiwa, Towa, Keresan, Zuni, and Hopi pueblos rose together against the Spanish from Taos to the Hopi mesas, three hundred miles of desert coordinated by a knotted string. The federation preserves the runner network as a standing institution: a corps of swift-runners trained from boyhood in every pueblo, knotted cords as the medium of inter-pueblo summons, and a coordinating council at the Taos pueblo.

conditions.text: Any of

list.name: Pecos Plains Trade
list.text: The eastern-frontier institution by which the easternmost pueblos (Pecos in particular, with Cuartelejo and Picuris) brokered exchange between the agricultural pueblo world and the bison-hunting peoples of the southern plains. At the autumn trade fairs, held at Pecos in October and Taos in summer, Apache de Cuartelejo, Jicarilla, and from c. 1700 Comanche and Wichita brought bison hides, dried meat, tallow, captives, and slaves in exchange for maize, beans, squash, woven cotton mantas, ground pigment, and the turquoise mined at Cerrillos. The pueblos collected tolls and a percentage of the through-traffic; Pecos grew wealthy as the gateway between two worlds. Spanish governors repeatedly tried to suppress the fairs and as repeatedly failed.
